words: step; first; next; last; order; follow; plan; algorithm
notes: Unplugged day. Children carry out everyday routines as ordered steps (washing hands, getting dressed, a snack line) and a made-up one (a robot dance), saying first, next, last. The word algorithm is taught in context: a set of steps in order that we follow is an algorithm. Introduces the step-card: one picture per step, laid left to right. Words are spoken and shown with pictures; nothing is read alone. This is the base row for every algorithm row after it.

words: make; design; invent; people; helper; rule
notes: Unplugged day. A person made each routine and each game rule, so a person can change it: the class changes one step of a working step-card set and checks what happens. With the teacher, children describe in simple words how a person makes an algorithm: choose a task, notice its smaller parts, put the steps in order to reach the goal (breaking a task into parts on one's own is grade 1's g1-split-task). Then children make a step-card set for a game they know, and a classmate follows it and says whether it worked. Tells the class that people design the tools around them (a spoon, a pencil, a game, a computer) and the steps they run: a person thought of a game's rules, drew its characters and programmed it. Part of this row is met by talk and drawing; no device needed.

words: command; program; forward; turn; left; right; blocks
notes: Unplugged first: a child moves a partner or a toy along a floor grid using arrow cards, then lays the cards in order as a program. Device day: the same short path built from large picture blocks in a block language, one block per step, run and watched. Introduces the block-program. A worked path is shown and traced before any child builds alone. Device versions follow STANDARD.md (one device per pair, stations, one screen, or paper arrow cards).

words: tell; describe; does; happens; because
notes: Given a short block program or an arrow-card line, children say aloud what it makes the character do, step by step, before it runs, then check by running or by walking it. Teacher notes the answer by exception. Reading is by picture only. Unplugged day with a device check; the paper path needs no screen.

words: bug; fix; wrong; broken; try again; test
notes: A given program that does not reach the goal (the toy stops short, turns the wrong way). Children point to the step where it first goes wrong and say what to change. Bug is taught with both meanings, an insect and a mistake in a program. Errors are normal and shared. Unplugged with arrow cards, or device day with a one-block fix.

words: sign; symbol; gesture; thumbs up; traffic light; means; choose
notes: Unplugged day. Everyday signs and gestures carry information that people use to choose: a red light, a thumbs up, a wave, an arrow, a clock hand. Children read pictured signs and gesture cards and say what each tells them to do. This is the first idea of a value that stands for something; no variable is taught. Spoken and pictured words only.

words: group; same; different; color; shape; size; pattern; sort
notes: Unplugged day. Children sort real objects and picture cards by one attribute (color, size, shape, wet or dry), find what the group has in common and then guess which group a new card belongs to. This is how machines that sort things first work, taught without the machine: notice what is the same, then decide. Introduces the attribute-cards. No device needed.

words: question; count; more; fewer; most; graph; answer
notes: Unplugged day. The class asks a question about its own room (which game, which weather, which class-library book) and collects the answers by placing a block or sticker per child on a floor or wall picture graph, then reads it to answer. The teacher poses the first question; children pose the next one from a picture prompt. Introduces the picture-graph. Class data is about things, tallied by hand; no child is named. Used again with every later data row.

words: choose; decide; because; plan; vote
notes: Unplugged day. The class uses its own picture graph to make a real choice (which game to play, which book to read) and says what the graph showed. Children name one other everyday decision that people make from counts (what to pack when it rains, what to cook). Said aloud and pointed to; teacher notes by exception.

words: tool; job; use; computer; tablet; button; screen; touch
notes: Unplugged and device day. Children match tools to jobs for different people (a spoon and a fork, a magnifier, a pencil grip, a screen reader, a keyboard) and name the parts of a device they touch or look at. Asks who a tool works for and who it does not, the first human-centered idea. Device version: a few devices at stations, or one screen with a child at the device for each step.

words: careful; share; turn; ask; kind; safe; rules
notes: Unplugged and device day. The class makes simple rules for using shared devices and tools (take turns, ask before using, handle with two hands, stop when told) and acts out a right way and a wrong way. Children say why each rule helps people. Said aloud; no reading.

words: public; private; share; secret; name; address; password
notes: Unplugged day. Children sort picture cards into what is fine to tell anyone (a favorite color) and what only family or a trusted adult should know (a home address, a password). No real personal detail is used or asked for. Introduces the idea that private things need protecting, which later rows turn into accounts and passwords.

words: home; school; work; use; device; helper; job
notes: Unplugged day. Children point out and name devices in pictures of a home, a school and a workplace (a store checkout, a clinic, a farm), and say who uses each and for what. No named products. Builds the sense that computing is part of many jobs.

words: before; after; then; now; change; old; new; long ago
notes: Unplugged day. Paired pictures of an older and a newer version of a computing device used at school or at home (a corded phone with push buttons and a flat touch-screen phone, a deep box-shaped screen and a flat screen, a large desk computer and a tablet) are put in order on a two-card strip, older on the left. Children say what looks different (smaller, flatter, no cord, a touch screen). Introduces the timeline as a short strip of then and now. No dates, inventors or how the parts work inside; comparing how an everyday activity was done before and after a technology arrived is grade 1's g1-then-and-now. No child is asked about the devices at home; a child's own offer is welcome.

words: break down; part; whole; step; list; task; goal
notes: Unplugged day. A bigger task (make a sandwich, tidy the room, build a block tower) is broken into small parts and each part into steps on cards. Children check by having a partner carry the cards out. Builds on the K step-card by adding the idea of parts of a task. The cards become the plan for the next programming row. Device version: not required; the idea is met unplugged.

words: change; different; result; swap; same; instead
notes: Unplugged day. A working step-card plan is changed (swap two steps, drop one, add one) and children predict what comes out differently, then check by carrying it out. Explains in a sentence that a change to the steps leads to a different result. Builds on K: a person made the plan, so a person can change it.

words: pattern; example; guess; sort; machine; learn; picture; data
notes: Unplugged day. Children sort picture cards, then play a guessing game where a partner who has seen a few examples guesses which group a new card is in by the pattern. Names the idea that some computer systems, made by people, find patterns in many examples to make a decision or make something new (a library screen that suggests a next book from the books read before; a drawing tool that makes a new picture from the patterns in many pictures). Said simply, with no claim that a machine thinks. The attribute-cards from K carry on.

words: number; count; word; describe; collect; ask; watch; record
notes: Unplugged day. The class collects both counts (how many chairs, how many sunny days) and descriptions (the color of a leaf, how a crayon feels) using asking, watching and measuring, and records each on a picture graph or a labeled card. Uses more than one way to collect, then answers a question with the mix. Number and word data are named as types in grade 2.

words: question; data; ask; answer; need; community; family
notes: Unplugged day. Children sort questions into those that counting or looking can answer (how many windows does our room have) and those of feeling, guess or imagination (which window has the best view). Then they look at questions people in the school or town might ask to meet a need (when does the bus come, which part of the school garden needs water, how many books the library needs for each class). Data work stays on class things, never on named children, and never on food, pets, homes or bodies. They also see how changing one word changes what a question asks and who it fits (which game do we like best, which game can all of us play).

words: code; event; start; when; sequence; character
notes: Device day, with an unplugged day first. Children turn a step-card plan from g1-split-task into blocks, including one event block (when this is tapped, start), and run it. The worked example is shown and traced before anyone builds alone. Paper stand-in: arrow cards with a start card. A text view of the same program is shown to the teacher only.

words: event; tap; press; what happens; because; order
notes: Children read a short given block program that starts on an event and say what it does and why, before running it. Predict, then run, then compare. The K idea that order matters returns with an event: nothing happens until the event. Spoken or pointed answers; no reading beyond icons.

words: debug; bug; find; fix; test; again; first wrong
notes: A given block program with one wrong step or one out of order. Children trace it, find the first step that is wrong, change one thing, and test again. This is the debugging method in four words: predict, run, find, fix. Unplugged with arrow cards on a floor grid, or device day.

words: change; stay the same; day; weather; height; age; count; time
notes: Unplugged day. Children sort pictured things by whether the value changes over time (the weather, a plant's height, the date, their age) or stays the same (a birthday, a name). This is a first look at a changing value without a program. Examples use plants, weather and clocks, not named people.

words: community; library; shop; clinic; use; digital; school
notes: Unplugged day. A picture tour of home, school and town: who uses a computer or a digital device there, and for what (checking out a book, paying, a map, a doorbell). Children draw one place and one use. No named products or companies.

words: before; after; compare; change; activity; invention; long ago
notes: Unplugged day. Take one everyday activity (talking to a faraway friend, finding a place, listening to music) and lay out how it was done before and after a technology arrived on the two-card timeline. Children say what got easier, faster or different. Facts about dates are from memory and are checked by the teacher before use.

words: good at; people; computer; fast; tired; creative; check; kind
notes: Unplugged day. Sort a set of activities into what people do well (comfort a friend, invent a game, notice a mood) and what a computer does well (add a long list fast, repeat the same step without tiring, store a lot). Some activities go in both. No claim that computers feel or think.

words: keyboard; mouse; screen; speaker; camera; hardware; part; job
notes: Unplugged and device day. Children name the basic parts of a device (screen, keyboard, mouse or touchpad, speaker, camera, microphone) with the right words and say each part's purpose. Match part to job on a pictured device and on the real one. One device per pair, or one on the class screen.

words: responsible; careful; share; ask; rules; kind; time
notes: Unplugged day. Children say what a responsible user does with shared devices and tools: asks first, takes turns, keeps things clean and safe, tells an adult when something seems wrong. They say why each rule exists, their own part in keeping it, and what happens to them and to the class when a rule is not kept. Acted out with a short story card, no real accounts. Builds on the K rules.

words: password; account; lock; safe; secret; share; adult
notes: Unplugged day. Introduces a password as a private key to an account and a lock as a picture. Children sign in and sign out of a pretend login on paper with a given pretend password (no child makes one up), watch the teacher sign out of the class device, sort what to share (a drawing) and what to keep private (a password), and say what to do if someone asks for it (say no, tell a trusted adult). No real account is made by any child.

words: repeat; loop; again; times; event; when; algorithm
notes: Unplugged day. Children write an algorithm that has an ordered sequence, one event (when the bell rings) and a repeat (clap three times) for a dance, a drawing or a game, then a partner follows it. The repeat shortens the step-cards: a card says repeat 3 and holds the steps that repeat. Builds on splitting a task into parts. Device version: not required.

words: fair; peer; different; people; needs; rule; game
notes: Unplugged day. A game's rules are an algorithm. Children play a game as written and notice who it works well for and who it leaves out (the rule that needs a fast runner), then say whether everyone had a fair chance and whether anyone might never get a turn. The same rule can work well for one child and badly for another. Judging fairness is the skill; designing a fairer rule is not asked in grade 2.

words: train; training; example; data; label; model; guess; wrong
notes: Unplugged day. A class sorter learns from labeled example cards: students act as the machine, look at the labeled examples (the training set) and then guess new cards. Children see that a guess is only as good as the examples it learned from, for instance when every example of a bird has wings spread. Introduces the training-set. A device sorting tool may be shown on one screen.

words: repeat; loop; event; sequence; code; command; run
notes: Device day, with an unplugged day first. Children turn the algorithm from g2-algorithm-loops into blocks with a sequence, an event and a repeat block. Worked example first and traced, then a version with blanks, then a modify, then a build. Paper stand-in: step-cards with a repeat card, acted out by a partner.

words: plan; build; test; change; steps; because; program
notes: Children say the steps they took to make a program: what the plan was, what they built first, what they tested, what they changed. Uses the sentence frame First I ___, then I ___. A finished program is shown and explained in order. Spoken or drawn, with the teacher noting by exception. Each child also says which part was their own idea and which part a classmate or the teacher helped with.

words: debug; loop; too many; not enough; fix; test; first wrong
notes: A given program with a bug in a repeat (it repeats too many times, an event does not start) or a sequence. Children predict, run, find the first place it goes wrong, change one thing and test. Devices or arrow cards on a floor grid. Tracing is by pointing and counting with fingers.

words: name; label; value; constant; changes; box; score; time
notes: Unplugged day. Children label things that hold information with a name and say whether the value stays the same or changes: the score, the date, the class plant's name, the time. A named box, a cup with a label, holds one value; a card shows what is inside. This is the first named-box. No variable is used in code yet; a score on a game screen is shown and labeled.

words: number; word; count; describe; table; row; column; collect
notes: Unplugged day. Compare number data (how tall) and word data (what color) in how each is collected (measure, ask, look) and what each tells. Both go into a two-column paper data-table. Introduces the data-table as rows and columns on paper. The picture-graph and the table are put side by side.

words: ask; question; fair; biased; sample; leave out; guess; collect
notes: Unplugged day. Children turn a vague question into one data can answer (what do kids like becomes which game does our class pick most for indoor recess), set aside a question that data cannot answer, then compare ways to collect (ask only the front row, ask everyone, ask by hand raise versus in secret) and say which could give a wrong or unfair answer and why. Uses class things only. A simple bias is named as leaving some people out. They say how a one-sided way of asking could lead to an unfair choice for the class, such as a game picked by the front row only.

words: career; job; interest; hobby; build; create; help; computer
notes: Unplugged day. Children connect something they like (animals, art, sports, music, cooking) to ways computing is used in jobs that involve it (a vet clinic record, a sound studio, a sports score system). Drawn and told; no company or product names.

words: culture; invent; long ago; problem; solve; tool; express
notes: Unplugged day. Familiar machines people made to solve everyday problems (a traffic light, an automatic door, a crossing signal that sounds for people who cannot see it) are matched to the problem each was made for. Case cards show people in different places and times who made a tool for counting, writing, mapping or making music to solve a problem or share an idea (the abacus; knotted cords for records; from memory, the teacher checks the sources). Children place the tools on the timeline and say what problem each solved. Shows that many people everywhere have designed computing tools.

words: input; output; processing; keyboard; screen; speaker; work together
notes: Unplugged and device day. Introduces the input-to-output picture, the system-diagram: an input part takes in, the computer parts do something, an output part shows or sounds. Children sort parts as input or output (a mouse is input, a speaker is output) and trace one action from a touch to a change on the screen.

words: good; harm; help; hurt; too much; screen time; choose
notes: Unplugged day. A two-column benefit-risk-chart, one side for how a tool helps and one for how it can hurt, for one pictured tool (a video call, a game, a drawing tool), so no child is asked about a device at home. Children add one thing each way and say what a person could do about the harm. Introduces the benefit-risk-chart.

words: online; post; share; real; forever; kind; hurtful; pretend
notes: Unplugged day. With a pretend page on paper, children see that what someone posts or sends is seen by real people and can be kept and passed on. Sort kind and unkind messages and say what happens next to the sender and the reader. No real account or message is made.

words: if; else; choose; decide; condition; algorithm; combine; repeat
notes: Unplugged day. Children write an algorithm that combines sequence, an event, a repeat and a choice (if it is raining, take the umbrella; else take a hat) for a game, a route or an act. Selection is introduced here with a yes or no question and two paths. A partner follows the written steps exactly, which shows where a step is missing. In-grade order for grade 3: g3-make-improve (block-and-text-view) before g3-read-code, then g3-variable-trace (trace-table), then g3-debug-combo.

words: fair; effect; compare; different; people; needs; outcome
notes: Unplugged day. Two ways of doing the same job (first come first served, or a time slot for each) are carried out on the class and compared by their effect on people with different needs (a student who needs more time, a student who is new). Children use a benefit-risk-chart per way. Builds on g2-algorithm-peers.

words: training set; add; new; change; better; model; same
notes: Unplugged day. A card sorter built from a small training-set is tested and then given more labeled examples and tested again. Children compare what it gets right before and after and say why it changed: adding examples of the kind it saw least helped. Run as a class game or, on one screen, with a simple sorting tool.

words: accurate; complete; missing; wrong; check; fix; number; word
notes: Unplugged day. A paper data-table with a few wrong entries and gaps (a missing cell, a height of 400 inches) is given. Children check it for accuracy and completeness, say which entries to ask about again and which to leave out. Number and word data are both checked. Device version: none required.

words: attribute; compare; relationship; scaled; more than one; investigate
notes: Unplugged and device day. A data-table with several attributes per row (weather, temperature and wind; a plant's height and its sunlight) is used to answer a question about how two attributes go together, with a scaled picture graph. Children say what they found and one thing the data cannot tell them.

words: survey; group; background; fair; include; question; collect; everyone
notes: Unplugged day. Children design a short class data collection (a survey on a topic that matters to the class) so that every kind of student can answer it: different languages, abilities, interests. They check the question and the way of collecting for anyone left out. No identifying details are gathered. The survey has a box for saying no, and children learn they may tell a teacher or a website that they do not want to share.

words: improve; feedback; plan; selection; if; text; blocks; version
notes: Device day, with an unplugged day first. Children write their own algorithm on step-cards (from g3-algorithm-combo), build it in blocks with a sequence, event, repeat and a choice, and trade it for feedback from a partner with a look-for list (does it do what the plan says, is it clear), then improve it. Introduces the block-and-text-view: the same program shown as blocks beside its text. Reading load is ten lines at most. Paper stand-in: written step-cards and a partner who carries them out. The feedback step (does it do what the plan says, is it clear) is the same habit as the writing process in the ELA course. Each program names who wrote the algorithm and who built it.

words: purpose; part; segment; read; trace; points; whole program
notes: Device and unplugged day. Given a short block program with the block-and-text-view beside it, children say what one part of it is for in the whole program (what would stop working if that part were removed) and trace the program by pointing at each step. There is no variable here and no trace-table; both come in g3-variable-trace. A worked example is read aloud first, then a partner pair reads a second one. Paper stand-in: the program printed as blocks and text, pointed at with a pencil. In-grade order: g3-make-improve, then this row, then g3-variable-trace, then g3-debug-combo.

words: variable; score; counter; value; store; change; trace-table; box
notes: Device and unplugged day. Given a short program with a score or counter, children name each variable, say what is stored in it and what changes it, and fill a trace-table by hand: one column per variable, one row per step. Introduces the trace-table. A variable is a named box that holds one value at a time; assignment is not equality, so x gets x plus 1 is read as take what is in x and put one more into it. Teacher notes the misconception. The labeled named-box on paper from g2-name-and-label becomes a variable in code. Comes after g3-read-code in the grade and before g3-debug-combo. The math lean (a letter standing for an unknown) may come later in the math year, so the teacher keeps the demand to one variable and a known starting value.

words: debug; selection; wrong branch; condition; trace; predict; fix
notes: A given program that mixes sequence, event, repeat and a choice has a bug (the choice tests the wrong thing; both branches run). Children trace with a trace-table, find the first wrong place, change one thing, retest. Devices or a paper program with a partner who runs it. Uses the trace-table of g3-variable-trace, which runs first in the grade.

words: industry; farm; hospital; shop; work; skill; tool; team
notes: Unplugged day. Case cards of workers in different industries (farming, health, building, shops, music) and the computing tool and skill each uses. Children match worker to tool to job and say what the job would be like without the tool. No named products. Cases are from memory, to be checked before use.

words: benefit; risk; family; community; personal; widely used; map; messaging
notes: Unplugged day. For a widely used system (a map app, a video call, a school login) children fill a benefit-risk-chart for personal and family life and say who in the community it touches. Real cases are told by what happened, never by company or product name. Builds on the benefit-risk-chart of grade 2.

words: invent; why; need; change; communicate; live; work
notes: Unplugged day. Pick two computing tools from different eras on the timeline (finding a fact, keeping in touch, paying at a shop, each at three times; and why a weather forecast, a route finder and a voice helper were built) and ask why someone made each and how it changed how people lived, worked or kept in touch. Facts about the tools are from memory, to be checked before use, and the check is recorded in the teacher source line.

words: software; app; program; instructions; hardware; task; update
notes: Unplugged and device day. Software is the instructions that tell hardware what to do. Children sort pictured things into hardware and software and trace one task (drawing a shape) from the program, through the device, to the screen, adding software to the system-diagram.

words: internet; network; connect; router; send; receive; message; website
notes: Unplugged day. Children act out how a message gets from one class to another through a chain of kids (devices) and a helper (a router), and draw it. Introduces the network-diagram: boxes for devices and lines for connections, with a labeled internet cloud meaning many other people's computers. Children say how people use the internet to find things and to talk.

words: personal; information; private; share; photo; name; address; post; safe
notes: Unplugged day with pretend pages on paper. Children judge which details in a mock profile or post could show who a person is or where they live (a school name, a photo of the street; a screen name or team name and game times in an online game; a pop-up that says you won a prize and asks for an address) and which are safe to share. They suggest a safer post. No real personal detail is used or posted.

words: group; disadvantage; benefit; algorithm; compare; fair; outcome
notes: Unplugged day. Two algorithms for the same job (picking teams, sharing a limited supply, ordering a line) are run on case cards of different groups, and the class evaluates who each helps or disadvantages and why. Children use a benefit-risk-chart per algorithm. Designing a new algorithm is left out: grade 4 compares.

words: property; training data; output; learn; machine; human; practice; examples
notes: Unplugged and one-screen device day. Change one property of a training-set (the examples are all one color, or too few) and predict then observe how a sorter's output changes. Then compare how a child learns a word and how a machine learns from labeled examples: people use meaning and a few examples, a machine needs many and has no understanding. Algorithm and society ideas share one row because they are taught as one story.

words: written; step; numbered; event; repeat; if; choice; start; end
notes: Unplugged day. A written algorithm with a sequence, an event, a repeat and a choice is set down in everyday numbered sentences, for example a choose-your-path story where the reader's choice sends them to a different step. The step-cards become written lines, and a pattern rule (add 3) is written with a repeat. Words only: no flowchart, diagram or pseudocode is asked here; the flowchart comes in g5-visual-algorithm. No programming language is needed.

words: computer tool; table; record; attribute; row; column; sheet
notes: Device day. Students enter collected class data into a table in a computational tool with one row for each record (a plant, a picture of a class object, a day's weather) and one column for each attribute, then sort a column. Part met without a device on the paper table: the same record and attribute idea, marked part met without a device. One device per pair or one screen with a student at the keys.

words: chart; bar; line; report; result; process; explain; claim
notes: Device and unplugged day. Students ask a question, collect the data, make a bar graph or chart from a table, and explain the process and what the graph shows in a few sentences with the chart attached. Introduces the data-visualization, built from the data-table. A hand-drawn chart is the paper version.

words: collected; about people; group; use; harm; help; privacy; fair
notes: Unplugged day. Case cards describe data collected about groups of people (a school survey, a map of where people travel, a store count). Children ask who is collecting it, what is collected and why, then say which person and which group could be helped or hurt, in plain words (helpful, harmful, unfair), shown on a data-table. Weighing whether the collection is good or bad overall is left out. No real children's data is used.

words: compare; correct; clear; solution; shorter; better; same result
notes: Device day. Two given programs reach the same result in different ways (a long and a short one, one that repeats a block, one that does not). Students compare them for correctness and clarity and say which is clearer for a new reader. Ten lines at most. Paper stand-in: two printed programs compared side by side.

words: team; driver; navigator; comment; document; explain; contribute; part
notes: Device day. Pairs and teams of three build one program with roles (driver at the keys, navigator reading and checking, switch on a timer). Each member adds a part and writes a short comment on what it does. A reader who did not write it checks the comment against the code. Roles switch every few minutes so no one holds the keys all period.

words: trace; value; change; flow; update; counter; store
notes: Device and unplugged day. Students trace how data flows through a program: which values go in, how each variable changes after each line, and what comes out. They fill a trace-table for a counting loop and for a score program and check by running. Predict first, then run, then compare.

words: test; small; one at a time; debug; incremental; check; part
notes: Device day. A program is built and run in small pieces, tested after each new part, and the bug is found because the last piece is the only change. Introduces the test-table: what I tested, what I expected, what happened. Students practice on a given buggy build and then on their own. Paper stand-in: a paper program and a test-table.

words: workforce; update; skill; learn; new tool; adopt; change
notes: Unplugged day. Case cards of workers whose jobs changed when a new computing tool arrived (an office, a farm, a clinic). Students say what the worker had to learn and how they kept learning. Sources are a dated teacher source line, not product names.

words: inventor; community; contribute; limit; next; improve; emerging
notes: Unplugged day. Biographies of diverse people and communities in the history of computing (from memory, checked in the teacher source line) go on the timeline with what each added. Students then name a limit of an existing tool (the battery runs out, the screen is too small) and how that limit led people to make something new.

words: troubleshoot; check; restart; plug; connect; problem; fix; hardware
notes: Unplugged and device day. A troubleshooting process in steps (what is wrong, is it plugged in, restart, try something simpler, ask) is used on staged faults that the class tries to find: unplugged mouse, volume off, wrong app. One device per pair or a toy device built from pictures.

words: energy; material; resource; environment; recycle; use; device; waste
notes: Unplugged day. Trace a device from material to use to throw away (energy in, metals and plastics in, waste out). Students list how widely used systems affect natural resources and the environment, and one thing a user can do (use it longer, repair, recycle).

words: wired; wireless; cable; signal; connect; compare; speed; range
notes: Unplugged day. Two network-diagrams of the same room (cable to the router; wireless to the router) are compared. Students list one way each is better (steady and fast; free to move), and act out the signal along a cable and through the air.

words: login; password; proves; permission; allowed; authentication; authorization
notes: Unplugged day. A building with a front door and rooms: showing who you are at the door is one thing (a password) and what you are allowed to open is another (a key for one room). Students sort cards as proving who someone is or deciding what they may do. Pretend accounts only. Teach login (proving who you are) and permission (what you may open) first; the long words authentication and authorization come last, after the cards are sorted.

words: user; need; design; test; improve; include; feedback; designer
notes: Unplugged day. Four human-centered design ideas, in plain words: ask who will use it, include different users, test with them, improve. Students take a given technology (a school app, a map) and find where each idea shows in it, then change one design for a user it leaves out. Students also name the considerations a designer weighs (user needs, accessibility, fairness) and the designer's own values; people make technologies, so a design can be unfair or wrong for some users.

words: train; model; classify; predict; accuracy; test set; data
notes: Device day. Students train a small classifier in a browser tool on shapes they draw on the tool's drawing pad (no camera or microphone) and test it on new examples, then look at what is missing from the training-set, add varied examples, retrain and compare counts out of ten. Part met without a device: the class sorts cards as a pretend model on paper, marked part met without a device. One device per pair, stations or one screen.

words: variable; counter; flowchart; event; decision; loop; update; value
notes: Unplugged day. A flowchart for a score game or a counting task starts on an event (when the start button is pressed), repeats a step, and uses a variable that changes each time round (score goes up by one) and a decision that reads it. Students build the flowchart from a plan, trace it with a trace-table and check against a partner's. Introduces the flowchart: the written steps of g4-written-algorithm become boxes, diamonds for decisions and arrows, with a variable box. Formal flowchart symbols are a help, not a demand; a drawing on index cards with branches does the same job.

words: sensor; form; sheet; collect; organize; type; number; text
notes: Device day. Students collect data of more than one type with a computational tool (a shared form on a pretend class survey, a sensor reading from a classroom thermometer) and organize it in a table. Students label each column numeric or descriptive, and sort and group in the tool. Part met without a device: paper form and hand tally, marked part met without a device.

words: variability; spread; outlier; cause; measure; typical; different
notes: Device and unplugged day. A given dataset (plant growth, sound levels, daily temperatures) is analyzed for how much values differ and where the differences may come from (measuring error, different conditions, real change). Students mark typical values and the outlier, say a possible source of the outlier, and name one relationship between two columns; no mean or other statistic is computed.

words: collected data; benefit; risk; purpose; trust; protect; limit
notes: Unplugged day. Case cards of a technology that uses collected data (a route planner, a recommendation list, a fitness count). Students fill a benefit-risk-chart and say who gains, who is at risk and one limit that would make it safer.

words: remix; combine; modify; existing; credit; new; idea
notes: Device day. Students start with a working program, modify it and combine it with a part of another to make a novel one, crediting the source in a comment. A worked remix is traced first. Ten lines at most. Paper stand-in: cut and paste a printed program into a new one.

words: component; assemble; comment; document; instructions; team; test
notes: Device day. Each student builds one component of a shared program and writes the description another student could use to put it in place (an inline comment and a short external note). The pieces are assembled and tested by a student who did not write them. Roles and the final test are named in advance.

words: strategy; trace; isolate; divide; test; hypothesis
notes: Device and unplugged day. Three strategies (trace by hand, test one part at a time, isolate by taking pieces out) are tried on given buggy programs in turn, with a test-table. Students say which strategy found the bug and why. Paper stand-in: printed program and trace-tables.

words: variable; compare; store; update; greater than; counter; score
notes: Device and unplugged day. Programs that store a value in a variable, compare it with a number and modify it (a score that goes up, a timer that counts down, a password that is compared with a typed guess). Students trace each with a trace-table before running it. The note that assignment is not equality is repeated.

words: collaborate; engineer; designer; tester; team; project; role
notes: Unplugged day. Case cards of how a team (a designer, a programmer, a tester, a user) work together on one tool, and cases of professionals in different fields (a wildfire team on one live map, a museum exhibit team) sharing work through common digital tools, and a short team role-play on building a class tool. Students say what each role adds and what goes wrong when one is missing.

words: emerging; decide; appropriate; limit; people first; choose; automate
notes: Unplugged day. Students decide, from case cards of real situations, when a computing technology is the right tool (counting votes, translating a menu) and when it is not (comforting a friend, deciding a punishment), using a benefit-risk-chart and one question: should a person decide this? Each claim carries two views and a dated source in the teacher line. Students also look at why a family might choose to use or not use a new device at home (cost, privacy, who in the family can use it), without saying whether the choice is right.

words: include; exclude; inclusion; culture; design; access; language; community
notes: Unplugged day. Cases where leaving a group out shaped a tool (a form that did not fit every name, a voice tool that did not hear every accent) and cases where including a group shaped it (a tool designed with the people who use it, such as captions or a keyboard for a language, made with its speakers), told by what happened, no names, with two views and a dated source for each (STANDARD.md "Real cases in society days"); and how culture and ways of living and working shifted with computing. Students list who was included or left out, what it changed, and one change they would make. Cases are from memory, to be checked before use.

words: storage; memory; processor; input; output; software; hardware; save
notes: Unplugged and device day. The system-diagram grows to four parts: input, processing, storage and output. Students trace a task (typing a note and saving it) through hardware and software and say where each part is. Same device options as earlier.

words: router; switch; cable; wireless; access point; modem; part; internet
notes: Unplugged day. Label the parts of a wired and a wireless network on a network-diagram (device, cable, switch, router, access point, modem) and say what each does. Children act the parts in a room and trace a message through them.

words: secret; correct; available; confidentiality; integrity; availability; protect
notes: Unplugged day. The three needs of protecting information (only the right people see it, it stays correct, it is there when needed) are taught as a triangle with a story for each side (a locked diary, a message changed on the way, a store that is closed). Introduces the cia-triangle. Students match threats to the side they hurt.

words: pseudocode; flowchart; procedure; control structure; loop; selection; model
notes: Unplugged day, then device check. Given a working algorithm in words, students model it two ways: a flowchart with a loop, a choice and a call to a named procedure, and pseudocode (plain-language lines, indented). Introduces pseudocode, built from the flowchart line by line. Students check the two models say the same thing by tracing one input through each. g6-procedures runs before this row, so students have already written a procedure; here they call one as a named step. In-grade order for grade 6: g6-variable-types (introduces the text-program) before g6-procedures and g6-inclusive-collab, which use it; g6-procedures before this row; this row (introduces pseudocode) before g6-careers-ct, which writes pseudocode lines.

words: verify; input; expected; actual; edge case; test; correct
notes: Unplugged and device day. Students choose test inputs for a given algorithm (a typical case, the smallest, the largest, a case that should fail) and fill a test-table of expected against traced result. A found mismatch sends them back to the algorithm, not the code. Paper stand-in: the same table on paper traced by a partner.

words: hypothesis; classify; predict; feature; pattern; rule; confidence
notes: Device and unplugged day. Given a small trained classifier and its training-set, students write a hypothesis for how it decides (which features count) and test it with new examples they choose. They compare their guess about the rule to what it does. The model is shown as a rule learned from data, not a mind. Part met without a device: hand-sorting cards as the model, marked part met without a device.

words: principle; user; need; accessible; present; missing; inclusive; evaluate
notes: Unplugged day. Six human-centered principles (empathy, accessibility, user needs, fairness, sustainability, accountability) are used as a checklist on an existing computing technology the class knows (a school sign-in page, a bus app). Students mark each principle present or missing with evidence from the screen or a user interview, and write the one missing thing that matters most. Students also say how multilingual users, users with disabilities and users with limited internet meet the design differently.

words: precision; granularity; metadata; unit; accurate; storage; question; timestamp
notes: Unplugged and device day. The same measurement (the temperature outside) is recorded to the whole degree, to a tenth, by the hour and by the minute, and the class compares what each could answer and what it costs to store. Metadata is data about the data (who, when, where, what unit). Students add metadata to a table and show a question that cannot be answered without it. On a device, students open the properties of a supplied photo file and find the time and place that were added without anyone typing them. Recording at several precisions is shown by the teacher; the skill is judging what each precision allows.

words: sort; filter; group; summarize; average; count; column; sheet
notes: Device day. In a spreadsheet-style tool, students sort, filter, group and summarize a structured table (a class-built set of weather or plant records) to answer three questions. Part met without a device: the same moves done by hand on a printed table, marked part met without a device. One device per pair, stations, or one screen with a student at each step.

words: missing; duplicate; error; clean; remove; fill; quality; option
notes: Unplugged and device day. A messy table (a missing value, a duplicate row, an impossible number, two spellings of one thing) is given. Students list the options for each problem (remove the row, fill with a typical value, ask again) and what each does to the answer, the cause of each problem, and how removing rows can leave a group out; no option is marked correct. This is the first of a set that grade 7 uses to improve training data.

words: metadata; personal data; collect; consent; trace; owner; privacy
notes: Unplugged day. A first look at what a record about a person includes beyond what they typed (when, where, which device), using invented profile cards. Students list who might want it and for what, and one benefit and one risk. Fully owned in grade 7; here only the first look, with no real data.

words: data type; number; string; Boolean; variable; store; assign; text
notes: Device day. Grade 6 shows blocks and text side by side. Students store a number, a string of text and a true or false value in variables, change and combine them in a short program (a running total, a maximum and minimum, a count, a type conversion, joined text), and trace it with a trace-table. Introduces the text-program as the same program in a text language, read beside the blocks. A typed value and a number are not the same thing (a quick error shows why). Reading load is twenty lines at most. The short programs include one loop and one choice, shown in blocks beside the text, so the first text a student reads already has a repeat and an if.

words: procedure; call; name; reuse; clear; repeat code
notes: Device day. A program with the same four lines written three times is rewritten with one named procedure and three calls. Students first trace the original and the shorter version, then fill blanks, then write one themselves. The need for a name that says what it does is taught with a bad name and a good one. Paper stand-in: the two versions on paper traced by a partner. Parameters and return values wait for high school (g9-optimize-procedures).

words: pair; roles; driver; navigator; listen; credit; include; feedback
notes: Device day. Pairs and teams build a short program with named roles that switch on a timer, a team agreement (everyone's idea is heard, everyone types), and a look-for list the team checks at the end. Teams reflect on who spoke, who typed and what they changed. This is the practice day carried through grades 6 to 12.

words: era; government; organization; community; individual; shape; first computers; network
notes: Unplugged day. Three eras in computing history (counting machines, mainframes, personal and networked computers) are placed on a timeline. For each, students list who shaped it: an individual, a community, an organization, a government (from memory, the teacher source line holds the dated sources). Students also say what moved each actor, how the actors influenced one another, and one present-day case. The ownership of the roles is the skill; names and dates are cited, not memorized.

words: decision; choice; fair; consequence; ethical; user; rule
notes: Unplugged day. Case cards where a person chose how to use a computing tool (copying a classmate's work, sharing a private photo, reporting a bug), beside decisions made in design (what data to collect, which algorithm, how results are read). Students name the ethical and social consequences for each person, with two views and a dated source per case, and say what a better choice would have been, and propose a more responsible use.

words: career; worker; pattern; decompose; model; test; problem; tool
notes: Unplugged day. Workers in different careers (a nurse, a farmer, a builder, a musician) are shown with a real problem they solve. Students find the computational thinking in it: break the problem into parts, spot a pattern, test an idea. They write the pieces as pseudocode lines.

words: requirement; user need; system; compare; cost; energy; impact; fit
notes: Unplugged day. Two computing systems that do the same job for different users (a phone and a desktop, a library kiosk and a home device) are compared against user needs and requirements, then for cost, energy and environmental effects. Students build a system-diagram for each and say which fits whom.

words: sensor; controller; actuator; industry; embedded; function; farm; factory
notes: Unplugged day. Computing devices in industries (a farm sensor, a factory arm, a hospital monitor, a store checkout, a car's control unit) are put on system-diagrams with input, processing and output. Students say what each does and what job it replaces or helps. Students choose the industry and device they study. Part of the work uses a simulator on one screen; paper cards are the stand-in.

words: packet; header; reassemble; route; order; lost; message; send
notes: Unplugged day. A long message is cut into numbered packets on cards, sent by different routes across the room by students acting as routers, and put back in order at the far end by number. A packet is lost and the receiver asks again. Introduces the packet-strip. Students model how information is broken up, sent and rebuilt and say what the numbers are for. Each packet card carries its part of the message in ones and zeros, since what travels is binary. Students name a cause of loss (a crowded link, interference, a broken part) and one way to lessen it (send again, take another route).

words: confidentiality; integrity; availability; protect; data; risk; secure
notes: Unplugged day. Three small cases, one per side of the triangle, are used to practice sorting a problem to the need it hurts (a leaked grade list, a changed score, a locked school site). Grade 7 owns the effects of ignoring the triangle; here it is used and repeated.

words: design; variable; type; number; text; input; output; algorithm
notes: Device day. Students design an algorithm with variables of more than one type (a quiz with a number score, a text answer and a true or false passed value; a unit converter) as a flowchart and pseudocode, trace it with sample inputs, then build it in text. The design and its trace are scored; the text build is practice. Text is the main view; blocks are a stand-in. The variable types come from g6-variable-types.

words: procedural; rule; data-driven; approach; justify; combine; problem
notes: Unplugged day. Four problems (compute a total, decide whether a move is allowed in a board game by rules, sort photos into groups, predict tomorrow's attendance) are given. Students choose step-by-step instructions, rule-based logic, a method that learns from data, or a mix, and justify each in a sentence. No claim that one method is always better.

words: example; nonexample; accuracy; bias; training; balance; improve
notes: Device and unplugged day. Students train a small classifier on a set they build (one class has far fewer examples, one has misleading backgrounds), measure its accuracy on a test set, then improve it by adding better examples and non-examples and measure again. Data quality options come from g6-data-quality, so DC-24 comes before this day. Paper stand-in: sorting cards as the model. Part met without a device for MS-ALG-ML-07: the sorting-card stand-in is marked part met without a device. Scored on testing, reading results and suggesting data changes; the tool retrains, students do not change the model.

words: algorithm; bias; harm; benefit; evidence; ethical; daily life; feed
notes: Unplugged day. Students examine algorithms they meet daily (video order, school grouping, a price sort) and at least one AI system (speech recognition that misunderstands some accents, face matching wrong more often for some groups) as cases with evidence of benefit and harm. Each case is told by what happened, with two views and a dated source, never by company. They write one sentence on who is helped and who is hurt.

words: axis; scale; bar; line; misleading; design choice; title; interpret
notes: Device day. The same table is graphed three ways (a truncated axis, a wide scale, a different chart type) and students show how each design choice changes what a reader concludes. They pick the fairest chart and say why. They also check which chart can be read without color and by a reader with low vision.

words: metadata; ownership; privacy; sovereignty; consent; benefit; risk; personal data; share
notes: Unplugged day. Using invented profile data, students explain benefits and risks of letting personal data and metadata be collected and used: useful features and also tracking and sale. They discuss who owns it, how consent works, and data sovereignty (data collected in one country but stored under another country's laws, and a community or a nation, a tribal nation among them, deciding how data about its people and land is collected and used), with two views and a dated source for each case. Metadata is the first idea, carried from g6-precision-metadata.

words: iteration; selection; variable; procedure; role; trace; purpose; analyze
notes: Device and unplugged day. Given a twenty-line text program, students mark the role of each loop, choice, variable and procedure in a margin note and predict output for two inputs before running. Notional machine: the computer does one line at a time, in order, exactly as written.

words: documentation; reference; example; function; syntax; look up; use; guide
notes: Device day. Students use the language's reference page (supplied offline in the page) to find and use a function they have not been shown, and a plain-words error-message guide used to find a bug's cause. Part met without a device: reading a printed reference page and writing the call by hand, marked part met without a device. Teacher page holds the finished solution.

words: test plan; change log; document; refine; purpose; recheck; fix
notes: Device day. A program is tested with a planned test-table, bugs are fixed one at a time, and each change is logged (what was wrong, what changed, what was retested). Students recheck that a fix did not break something that worked (a bug that comes back after a fix); the statistics word regression is not used. The log is a few lines per change. Students also refine the program's prompts and messages, use code review feedback, test one procedure alone and watch a variable.

words: intended; unintended; impact; society; environment; invention; effect; era
notes: Unplugged day. Pick one historical computing technology (the telephone exchange, the personal computer, a large database) and trace its intended effects and its unintended side effects on people and on the environment on a timeline with two arrows (from memory, the teacher source line holds dated sources).

words: capability; limit; environmental; energy; appropriate; automate; judgment; decide
notes: Unplugged day. A set of tasks (grade essays, recognize handwriting, sort mail, decide a punishment) is judged for when AI, a robot, virtual reality or another emerging technology is suitable, by its strengths, limits, environmental cost, and the infrastructure and readiness it needs. Students use a chart with two columns and a verdict, and a person-decides flag for tasks that need a human. Builds on g6-human-decisions.

words: automation; replace; create; job; skill; retrain; worker; change
notes: Unplugged day. Case cards of jobs changed by automation (checkout lines, bank tellers, farm machines): which tasks were replaced, which jobs were created and what workers had to learn. Students weigh two views with a dated source for each, from memory checked by the teacher.

words: resilient; redundant; router; switch; server; client; path; failure; connect
notes: Unplugged day. A network map of nodes is given. Students remove one node, then a link, and show how packets find another path; they name the role of routers, switches and servers and say why more links make the network harder to break. Builds on the packet-strip.

words: breach; leak; tamper; outage; effect; consequence; protect; data
notes: Unplugged day. Cases (told by what happened, no company names) where one side of the triangle was ignored: a database left open, a record changed without a trace, a service down. Students explain the effect on people, using the confidentiality, integrity and availability words. Cases are from memory, to be checked before use.

words: access; ability; income; location; language; barrier; inclusive; connect
notes: Unplugged day. Students examine how access to the same system differs by physical ability, home internet, language, cost and place, using one local case (a library kiosk, a school portal) and a chart. They list barriers and who each one affects.

words: list; item; index; position; first; length; add; remove
notes: Device day. A list of values (names of plants, scores) is a named box with numbered slots. Introduces the list-diagram. Students add, read and remove items and loop over a list, tracing by hand. Text is the main view; blocks are shown as a stand-in for a student who needs them. Index counting starting at zero is taught as a convention with a worked example. Lists go past the middle school boundary (not expected until HS-PRO-VD-16, grade 9); kept, and these days count as days outside the standards under bar criterion C1's 10 percent (Cory, 2026-11-21, Desk q-fix-cs-2).

words: code review; comment; roles; peer; read; kind; clear; suggestion
notes: Device day. Pairs write and swap short text programs for a peer code review with a kind, specific checklist (what works, one thing unclear, one test to add). Roles still switch on a timer, and every student types in every session.

words: group by; summary; count; average; filter; sort; question; tool
notes: Device day. A larger table (a class-built weather log of fifty rows) is grouped and summarized with a tool to answer new questions, so the student sees what the same moves do on more data. Part met without a device: a printed fifty-row table worked by hand.

words: requirement; user; budget; compare; choose; fit; spec; tradeoff
notes: Unplugged day. Given a family or small shop with needs and a budget, students write requirements for a computing system and compare two options on a system-diagram, naming a tradeoff. The environmental effect of each is added.

words: assist; generated; check; prompt; output; verify; limit; own work
notes: Teacher-run on one screen with a tool the school has approved and no student accounts, or on saved outputs that Curio Class supplies. Students propose a prompt for a small programming problem, the class runs it, and students judge the output against the problem. A school with no approved tool marks the id part met. A student never types into or makes an account with a tool.

words: feature; limitation; accuracy; false positive; error; evaluate; test set; bias
notes: Device and unplugged day. Given a trained classifier and its test results, students list what it does well and where it fails (which kind of example is wrong most), name a feature that explains it and one thing it cannot do. A model is like a function: an input goes in and an output comes out, with errors. Students read a short model card supplied in the page (what it was trained on, where it should and should not be used, the computing it needs, its risks) and check the card against the test results.

words: bias; fair; change; rule; modify; impact; test; algorithm
notes: Device and unplugged day. A given algorithm (a sign-up lottery with a rule that favors the first to arrive) is traced on cases, a harm is named, then students modify the rule in pseudocode or text and retest on the same cases to show the change.

words: relationship; scatter; trend; predict; classify; variable; association; tool
notes: Device day, owned in grade 8 because the math frame teaches association here (math grade 8 unit 4, days 56 to 69). Students use a tool to find a relationship among variables in a table (a scatter of study time and score from a made-up set) and use it to make a prediction or classification. Part met without a device: plotting the points by hand.

words: investigation; summary; limit; evidence; bias; claim; source; process
notes: Device and unplugged day. Students write a short summary of a data investigation they did: question, method, data source, result, limits and possible biases. A given summary with an overreaching claim is graded against the evidence.

words: stage; collect; clean; label; bias; misleading; model; decision
notes: Unplugged day. Follow one dataset through its stages (collect, clean, label, summarize, train) and at each stage place a decision that can bias it, such as who was asked, which rows were dropped, how a label was chosen. Students show how that carries into a misleading chart or a poor model. Cases are from memory, to be checked before use.

words: accuracy; usable; generated code; test; review; bug; requirement; reliable
notes: Supplied saved code samples, some right and some flawed, for a given requirement. Students read each, run the test-table on it, and judge accuracy and usability, naming the first wrong line. No student uses a live generated-text tool; the answer key holds each sample's flaw. Students check that every function a sample calls really exists and suggest one change that would make it clearer.

words: attribution; credit; license; own; copy; intellectual property; permission; cite
notes: Unplugged day. Students decide, on cases (copying a function, remixing a project, using an image), when credit and permission are needed and write the credit line for a program that uses a function from another person's code. License terms are taught plainly. From memory, the teacher checks license examples before use.

words: feedback; usability; accessibility; user; refine; test; color; keyboard
notes: Device day. A small program is tried by two classmates, who give feedback on usability and accessibility (can it be used by keyboard alone, is it readable without color). Students refine it and re-test with them.

words: design decision; community; experience; different; emerging; voice; language; fair
notes: Unplugged day. A given emerging technology (a speech tool, a map route tool) is examined by how a design decision (which accents it was trained on, which streets it knows) changes the experience for different communities, with a dated source.

words: debate; local; community; social; cultural; environment; claim; rebuttal
notes: Unplugged day. A structured debate about a local effect of an emerging technology, with two prepared sides, a dated source for each and a rule that every claim is backed. Students debate the impact on the social, cultural and environmental life of their town.

words: phishing; malware; password; attack; prevent; update; backup; social engineering
notes: Unplugged day on toy systems built into the page. Students match common attacks (a fake message asking for a password, a program that hides inside another, a guessed password) to the triangle side they hurt and to a prevention. No real scanning, no attack on any real system and no real account. A cybersecurity vocabulary page is supplied.

words: diverse; improve; accessible; user; design; collaborate; feedback; need
notes: Device and unplugged day. A team takes a given system (a school sign-up page) with a barrier found in g7-access-differences, proposes a design change for different users, and tests it with teammates against each user's stated needs (keyboard only, enlarged text, no color, plain words), never by acting out a disability.

words: system; requirement; choose; compare; tradeoff; justify; cost; environment
notes: Unplugged day. Students choose between two systems for a school office using requirements written by the class, including a note on energy and a note on ethics. A short written justification is checked against the requirements. The requirements are written by a different group than the one choosing (grade 7, g7-system-requirements, wrote them for a given family or shop), and the justification is checked line by line against them.

words: failure; cut; reroute; backup path; resilience; node; link; outage
notes: Unplugged day. A new map and a new failure (a cut link, a down server) are traced through and students redraw the path packets will take. New task after g7-internet-resilience (find another path around a failure): students redraw the whole map and add a backup link so the failure no longer cuts anyone off. The idea is returned to in the high school network days.

model_in: text-program; list-diagram; named-box; flowchart; pseudocode; trace-table
model_out: text-program; list-diagram; named-box; flowchart; pseudocode; trace-table
words: project; design; plan; list; variable; procedure; trace; test
notes: Device day. A multi-week text project (a quiz, a small game or a data tool) in which students design with a flowchart and pseudocode, build in text with variables, a list and a procedure, trace the key part and hand it to a partner to read and explain. The list in this project goes past the middle school boundary; kept, and the list work counts as days outside the standards under C1's 10 percent (Cory, 2026-11-21, Desk q-fix-cs-2).

words: history; effect; policy; case; evidence; harm; benefit; source
notes: Unplugged day. A single case from the history of a computing technology is reread with the question of what a rule or law could have done earlier. The class adds this to its timeline and lists which later technologies the lesson applies to. The case: credit records before the Fair Credit Reporting Act of 1970 (FTC page on the Act).

words: career; skill; plan; interest; pathway; tool; training; change
notes: Unplugged day. Each student sketches one career path involving computing (their own interest), the skills it needs and how the work may change with automation. Students share at the level of ideas, not personal detail. The career thread (one short row a year, grades 8 to 12) stays in computer science; the career courses may point to it (Cory, 2026-11-20).

words: data structure; list; key-value record; record; index; key; store; access
notes: Device day. Students write programs that store, find and change data in lists and in key-value records (a roster of animals, a gradebook of made-up scores), tracing each with a list-diagram and a trace-table first. This comes before g9-design-with-structures in the year. Text language only. In-grade order for grade 9: this row before g9-design-with-structures (it writes its design against the structures taught here), and g9-modular after both. Dictionary here is a different thing from the data dictionary of g9-data-dictionary; this row says key-value record.

words: design; data structure; search; sort; choose; store; algorithm; efficient
notes: Device and unplugged day. Students pick a structure for a problem (a list for an order, a key-value record for lookup), design the algorithm in pseudocode and a flowchart, and justify the structure. A problem solved two ways shows how structure changes the steps. Placed after g9-structures-program in the year, same grade.

words: optimize; procedure; parameter; abstraction; repeat; loop; simplify; reuse
notes: Device day. A working but long program is rewritten using procedures with parameters and the right control structure, with the same output checked by the same tests. Students explain what each procedure hides and what its name promises.

words: deterministic; probabilistic; random; same input; same output; chance; simulate
notes: Device and unplugged day. A dice-based and a rule-based algorithm are compared: run the same input several times and record. Students say which is deterministic (same output every time) and which probabilistic, and one use of each (a spreadsheet total against a recommended list or a game dice roll). Probability comes from the math course. Builds on g8-ml-evaluate (an output that differs and errs), not on the one-screen generated-text day.

words: supervised; unsupervised; classify; predict; cluster; generate; algorithm type; task
notes: Unplugged day. Three task cards (sort mail, group customers by habit, write a caption) lead to a tour of AI algorithm types, matching the type to the task. Owned in grade 10; here students meet the names and the first matches.

words: bias; rule-based; data-driven; impact; harm; audit; evidence; fairness
notes: Unplugged day. A rule-based algorithm and a data-driven one are audited on the same cases, and students compare where each could discriminate. Owned in grade 11; grade 9 only introduces auditing a rule-based case.

words: simulate; parameter; random; model; generate; range; seed; assumption
notes: Device day. Students use a tool to generate a simulated dataset that matches stated parameters (values in a stated range, dice rolls) and check it for the stated range, then feed it into a short supplied simulation (a queue or a game of chance) and see how changing a parameter changes the result. Part met without a device: dice and cards generate a small simulated set by hand, marked part met without a device.

words: data dictionary; attribute; type; allowed value; relationship; field; unit; definition
notes: Unplugged and device day. For a given table students write a data dictionary: each field's name, type and allowed values, plus the rule between two fields (end date after start date). Another student tries to enter a bad row against the dictionary. The words data dictionary stay whole; a dictionary in a program (g9-structures-program) is a different thing.

words: large scale; privacy; collect; analyze; society; environment; consent; scale
notes: Unplugged day. Case cards of large-scale collection by a public agency or a store chain (told by what happened, no names) with the first look at who benefits and who is exposed. Here the first look. Hands on to g11-data-scale-ethics, which owns the id. Cases are from memory, to be checked before use.

words: module; procedure; library; object; reuse; read; interface; name
notes: Device day. A program is split into modules with procedures, a library function and a small object that holds data and actions, so each part can be read and reused. Part met without a device: the same split on paper, marked part met without a device. A solution key shows the split for every program.

words: trajectory; social factor; environmental factor; development; adoption; spread; policy
notes: Unplugged day. One computing technology (satellite positioning, from its start as a defense project to phones) is followed along a timeline with the society and environment factors that pushed or slowed it, each with a dated source in the teacher line. Students read two short supplied secondary sources and back each factor with one of them.

words: emerging; established; difference; capability; limit; compute; compare; influence
notes: Unplugged day. An emerging technology is set against the established one it may replace (quantum computing against classical computing, kept qualitative), and students list the technical differences and how each changes what the system can and cannot do.

words: operating system; manage; memory; file; process; peripheral; hardware; software; layer
notes: Unplugged day. An operating system is a manager between programs and hardware. Students act it out on cards (memory slots, a file shelf, a queue of tasks, and peripherals such as a keyboard, a printer and a sensor, each reached through a driver card) and add an OS layer to the system-diagram. A toy OS page is supplied.

words: capability; limit; sensor; memory; speed; battery; simulate; fit
notes: Device day. Students test a physical or simulated device against a task (a counter that should handle ten events a second) and say what it can and cannot do. Part met without a device: a paper simulator that students step through, marked part met without a device. A physical board is optional.

words: encryption; lock; backup; physical; policy; tradeoff; convenience; protect
notes: Unplugged day on toy systems built into the page. Students compare security measures (long passwords, a second check, a locked room, a backup) and the cost of each to users, data and devices. No scanning or attack on a real system.

words: network; diagram; hardware; software; protocol; client; server; link
notes: Unplugged day. Read before write: students read a given school network diagram (devices, the hardware and the software on each) and trace one request through it, saying what each device does with it. Drawing a network from a description is owned in g10-network-diagram, so nothing is drawn from scratch here.

words: career; goal; skill; pathway; interest; plan; field
notes: Unplugged day. Students list a goal, the computing skills it needs and one next step, kept private by default. Owned in grade 12.

words: efficiency; correctness; clarity; test case; steps; compare; count; metric
notes: Device and unplugged day. Two algorithms for the same task (a search that checks every item and one that halves the list) are compared by counting steps on growing inputs, by test cases and by how clear they are. Placed after the design and optimize days of g9.

words: supervised; unsupervised; neural; justify; task; data; type; limit
notes: Unplugged day. For each task card students choose an AI algorithm type and write the justification in two sentences using the task, the data available and the cost of an error. A selection that suits a different task is the wrong example.

words: human-centered; user research; persona; prototype; test; iterate; need; include
notes: Device and unplugged day. A team designs a small computing technology (a sign-up app, a kiosk screen) with the human-centered steps: interview a user, write needs, sketch, test, change. User stand-ins are persona cards read aloud, never acted. Students name the laws that set accessibility requirements for schools and public sites, by their government names, as a design constraint.

words: clean; text; case; whitespace; duplicate; format; normalize; tool
notes: Device day. Messy text data (a made-up volunteer sign-up list with spelling and spacing differences) is cleaned and organized with a tool, using find and replace, trim and sort, then removing duplicates, splitting one combined field into two and putting dates into one format. Part met without a device: hand-cleaning a short printed list, marked part met without a device. Students also say where a pattern rule (a regular expression) could find every case at once, without writing one.

words: consistent; valid; range; type; compliance; check; verify; rule
notes: Unplugged and device day. Students compare approaches to checking that data follows a dictionary (check each entry as it is typed, check the whole table after, check against a second source) and judge each on cost and the errors it catches.

words: parameter; return value; data structure; segment; analyze; trace; call; role
notes: Device and unplugged day. Given a twenty-line text program with a procedure that returns a value and takes a parameter, students explain what each part does and trace a call with a list. The assumption that the computer follows exactly what is written is repeated. After g9-modular. One saved code sample is also read and traced in this row, as a first look at HS-PRO-RD-18 (owned in grade 11, g11-evaluate-generated-code); no live tool. g8-evaluate-ai-code returns here after a skip of grade 9: students judged saved samples in grade 8, and grade 9 has no row that reads generated code, so this row reopens the habit before it is owned.

words: library; API; documentation; call; parameter; return; example; read
notes: Device day. Students read the documentation of a supplied offline library and use it to add a feature to a program, then explain what the documentation told them. Part met without a device: a printed documentation page used to write the call on paper, marked part met without a device. Students credit the library and the documentation page in a comment above the call, a first look at HS-PRO-PD-14 (owned in grade 12, g12-attribution). g8-attribution returns here after a skip of grade 9: the credit line of grade 8 now applies to a library, which grade 9 only used. Students also use the editor's step-through trace as a development tool.

words: inequity; access; environment; outcome; emerging; impact; energy; fair
notes: Unplugged day. A given emerging technology, written as a case card with no product named, is evaluated for its effects on society and the environment, with attention to who gains access and who does not. Each claim carries two views and a dated source, and students name the claim with the weakest evidence. Left out: predicting how the technology will develop. Paper path: case cards and a benefit-risk-chart on paper. Model carried: benefit-risk-chart.

words: choice; design; deploy; regulate; risk; long-term; responsible; harm
notes: Unplugged day. Four decision points (use, design, deploy, regulate) are applied to one case card. Students list at each point a risk, a benefit and a long-term effect, each with the view of a different person affected, and say which decision mattered most and why. Left out: deciding who was right. Paper path: a four-column benefit-risk-chart filled in pairs. Model carried: benefit-risk-chart. Case: Michigan's automated unemployment fraud system (2013 to 2015), from the Michigan Supreme Court's 2022 opinion in Bauserman v. Unemployment Insurance Agency, with an invented data-driven case card.

words: diagram; protocol; server; client; hardware; software; layer; address
notes: Unplugged day. Students diagram a network of a small office with hardware and software (devices, router, server and the programs on each) and trace one request through it.

words: internet; network of networks; address; route; protocol; ISP; local network
notes: Unplugged day. Several small networks are joined on the map, and students trace a packet between two of them. They describe how the internet differs from one office network (nobody runs the whole thing; many networks agree on rules). They name, at a high level, the layers a message passes through, the shared rules (TCP/IP) and the client and server roles. The packet-strip from g8-network-failure returns here; grade 9 skips it.

words: breach; cause; impact; phishing; social engineering; classify; community; government
notes: Unplugged day. Case cards of breaches and social engineering attacks (told by what happened, no names) are classified by cause (a weak password, a trick that fooled a person, an unpatched system) and by impact on an individual, an industry, a community or a government. Depth: classify and explain, no attack steps. Paper path: cards sorted on a grid. Model carried: cia-triangle. Cases: an invented hospital breach (invented for practice) and cases from the HHS Office for Civil Rights breach report page and CISA's social engineering page, checked there when the unit is written. Impacts are sorted by kind as well as by who: money, trust, legal and the work that stops.

words: policy; law; innovation; risk; ethical; propose; history
